News.title: ‘Giga chad’ influencer said he feels ‘like I’m dying every second’ in chilling vid before leaping into lake and drowning
News.content:
LATE influencer “looksmaxxer” appeared admitting he feels “like I’m dying every second” in a chilling video prior to his sudden death.

Fitness influencer, Connor Murphy, 32, drowned in a lake after running erratically from police in Samut Prakan province, near Bangkok, on July 7.



The self-described Giga Chad appeared panicked in a video which has gone viral since his death.

He said: “I’m really high. It’s getting weird.



“I feel like I’m dying every second.

“I’m just making this video so I can watch it and remind myself, Am I dreaming? Is it real?”

read more world news STRANGE ACTS Odd posts from 'giga chad' influencer Connor Murphy before death revealed

The video, titled “Obituary Pending” has now reached over 2.6 million views.

The full caption read: “Obituary Pending. This is purely a satirical acting performance. This dramatization does not depict any true events.



“Nothing in this video should be replicated and everything performed abides by all laws and regulations.”

The video began being re-shared after the news of his death broke.

A YouTuber, named Call Me Koosh, falsely labeled it – “last message to the world before his death.”



It is understood the video was in fact posted several years ago.

This comes as the influencer’s apartment was discovered in a state of squalor following his death.

Images and video reveal overflowing bags of trash, empty pill packets, discarded plastic bottles and food containers.



At least two walls around framed artwork were smeared with an unidentified yellow and black substance, believed to be paint.

The fitness YouTuber had amassed nearly 3m followers online by sharing content about his bodybuilding routine with snippets of comedy and philosophy.

A Giga Chad is an internet slang term for an ultra-masculine and attractive male figure, often used in manosphere communities.

Cops were called to Murphy’s apartment on Tuesday following reports of a man screaming.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Upon arrival Murphy fled to a nearby golf course where they found him swimming in a lake.



He is believed to have drowned after suffering leg cramps.

News.title: Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament crowned the UK’s best views, new poll finds
News.content:
PICTURE PERFECT Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament crowned the UK’s best views, new poll finds

BIG Ben and the Houses of Parliament have been crowned the UK’s best view, according to a poll.

The London landmarks topped the list, with 38 per cent of the 2,000 Brits surveyed selecting these as the most iconic sites.



Those polled chose them due to their instantly recognisable silhouette (67 per cent) and post-card worthy setting (26 per cent).

Fellow London vista Tower Bridge (36 per cent) followed closely behind.



Those who voted for the folding spectacle citing its famous landmark status (60 per cent) and international fame (58 per cent), which helped to cement the capital’s dominance in the national ranking.

The research, commissioned by Samsung, which will be unfolding innovative new form factors live from Galaxy Unpacked in London on July 22nd, also uncovered favourites from other UK regions including Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland (21 per cent).

As well as the towering sites of Arthur’s Seat in Edinburgh (13 per cent) and St Michael’s Mount in Cornwall (12 per cent).

Elsewhere, the natural arch of Durdle Door in Dorset (12 per cent), the rugged Cheddar Gorge in Somerset (12 per cent), and hidden gem Glencoe, Scotland (10 per cent) also proved popular picks.

Meanwhile, 25 per cent say they will post a beautiful view on social media within hours of finding it, underlining just how quickly Britain’s beauty spots are making their way online.

Nearly half admitted (49 per cent) they have travelled to an area primarily because they had seen photos or videos of it online, with social media the most likely platform to inspire those trips (64 per cent).



For younger Brits, the internet is no longer just inspiring the itinerary, it is setting it.

This is shown by the 80 per cent who have visited somewhere after seeing it online, more than three times the number of Boomers (25 per cent).

They are also over four times more likely to seek out iconic city skylines when travelling (25 per cent vs six per cent).

When it comes to getting the all-important picture, the research suggests amateur photographers want more control at their fingertips.

The findings, conducted to spotlight Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 7 and its Photo Assist feature, which makes it easier to remove unwanted background distractions, revealed 28 per cent would find the ability to remove people from photo backgrounds most useful.



Another 24 per cent added they would most value being able to remove unwanted objects from their pictures.

News.title: Twisted ‘sex attack’ letter landed my innocent pal in jail & ripped his life apart – it could happen to anyone
News.content:
AS chief of the local fire station, David Bryant was a well-known, respected and likeable figure in the small town of Christchurch, Dorset.

Recognised in the streets from various positive newspaper articles, he had been awarded the ‘Freedom of the Town’ for his work and everyone thought he and his wife, Lynn, were a close and loving couple.





“They were living life to the full, really, until 2012, when their world fell apart,” says close friend Simon Stanley, who was a firefighter at the station where David was his boss.

Then, a letter posted through David and Lynn’s door ended their contented life in the most nightmarish way.

It was from a man who accused David of having raped him as a teenager 35 years earlier. Now he was seeking justice.

David vehemently denied it but, in court, it came down to one man’s word against another. He was found guilty and sent to prison.

But as his family and friends set about fighting the conviction, a detail about his accuser came to light that would eventually turn the whole case on its head and clear David’s name once and for all.

The extraordinary story is told in the Channel 4 documentary, The Accused: Beyond Reasonable Doubt?

Diagnosed with dementia, sadly David is now too ill to speak about his ordeal, but in an exclusive interview with The Sun, his close friends, married couple Simon and Alex, talk about how the accusation, without any evidence, sent an innocent man to jail.

David’s nightmare began when the bombshell letter was hand-delivered in October 2012, the day after the Met Police launched Operation Yewtree, an investigation into historic sex crimes, in the wake of the Jimmy Savile abuse scandal.





Simon’s wife, Alex, was a friend of Lynn’s, and had met Simon through her. The foursome became good friends.

David was Simon’s best man at their wedding and he and Lynn were godparents to their daughter, Grace.

It was Alex who a shell-shocked Lynn turned to in the immediate aftermath of the letter arriving.

“That afternoon, Lynn phoned to say, ‘Can we come round?’” Alex recalls. “Something in her voice didn’t sound right. She was normally upbeat. When they arrived, she showed me the letter.”

It read: “Dave, it’s Danny Day. 35 years ago I used to collect the glasses in the Legion and I am the one that you and Spindel played darts with in the fire station. Remember?

“At 6 o’clock tonight I’m going to the police station to report what went on. And at 7 to the national papers. I think it’s time you and me had a chat. I think it is in your interest to call. One way or another, you will pay for what you have done in late ’76 to early ’77.”

“Dave was in shock,” says Alex. “He had no idea who Danny Day was and couldn’t think of anything that had happened in the past to warrant this.”

In his police interview, Day told them that he had been a teenager, collecting glasses at the local British Legion club in 1976 where he met Dave Bryant and his fellow firefighter colleague, Dennis ‘Spindel’ Goodman.



They had suggested he join them for a game of darts at the fire station and when he got there, he claims he was forcibly held across a table where he was raped by both men.

When asked why he had decided to come forward about it now, he said it was because of: “This Jimmy Saville thing about all these poor people that he’s been around. I can’t help thinking that it wasn’t only me. There must have been other people involved in this, other youngsters. And some maybe aren’t as strong as me.”

“Dave and Lynn thought this was just somebody on the bandwagon and it was blackmail to get money, so they decided they would go to the police straight away,” says Alex.

David eventually recalled Danny from the British Legion but said he had no recollection of the darts match at the station and he was insistent that he had no sexual contact with him whatsoever.

Despite there being no evidence, David was startled to find himself charged with rape.

Dennis ‘Spindel’ Goodman’s behaviour and reputation were at polar ends to that of David’s. He had been discharged from the fire service for sex offences and had died in 2003.

“There was something about my Uncle Dennis that I never liked and when he was discharged, I realised my gut feeling was right about him,” says his niece, Julie Goodman. “But Dave was not like that. He didn’t have a bad bone in his body.”

At David Bryant’s trial in December, 2013, Alex was startled to find herself sitting next to Danny Day.



“It was bizarre and horrible,” she says. “He was often muttering under his breath.”

There were some inaccuracies in Danny Day’s statement. He said he thought he had been raped across a pool table, but a pool table was not installed until 1992. He also mentioned walking through a fire exit which was not there until several years later.

“It’s a small fire station and anyone can easily walk by it and see the pool table through the window downstairs, and the emergency exit,” says Simon.

“Apparently the rape happened on a Thursday night, which has always been drill night at the station, so multiple people would have been there from six o’clock.”

Despite this, the jury found David guilty and he was sentenced to six years.

“I was absolutely flabbergasted that the jury believed Danny Day,” says Alex.

“Lynn and I had done some research into his background and on Companies House found he had set up so many companies that had failed.

“It was obvious he was trying to make money by accusing David. He didn’t come across as credible at all, in court, in my opinion.

“David doesn’t show emotion. Simon’s the same. When you’re in the fire service for so long, you see so many different incidents, some that you would rather not see, that you kind of put your emotions in a box and get on with things.

“David can’t show he is weak. He has to get a hold of a situation and deal with it on his terms. I think that lack of visible emotion almost went against him in police interviews and in court.



“He’d do anything for you and never had a bad word to say about anybody. You could rely on him if you needed help. He’d be the one person that you would always call for anything. He was a lovely, lovely guy and nobody had a bad word to say about him.”

Danny Day’s legal team went on to appeal the sentence, arguing it had been too lenient and they managed to get it increased to a minimum term of eight years.

“We would visit Dave in prison once a month on a Saturday,” says Simon. “He enjoyed the banter with me and others from the fire service but as soon as we got up to leave you could see the emotion in his face change, which was unlike him. And you could see a tear drop, because he knew he couldn’t come with us.”

While in Dartmoor prison, David met an inmate named Chris White, who had been convicted of rape in Bournemouth. Coincidentally, he knew Danny Day.

In his police statement, Day had said that he had told Chris White about having been raped by David Bryant and Dennis Goodman and that he had replied, “I always knew there was something not quite right with them.”

Mark Hensleigh, David Bryant’s solicitor, visited Dartmoor to talk to White where he categorically denied any such conversation with Danny Day took place.

“That was Lynn’s ray of hope then,” says Alex. “She said they were going to appeal and try to get Dave out.”

It was ten months into his sentence when David received a letter from lawyers acting for Danny Day, demanding compensation.



Day had had already received £11,000 from the criminal injuries commission but the decision to sue David in the high court was to prove his undoing.

The court requested Danny Day’s medical records, which were disclosed to David’s defence team. What was in them, was a bombshell.

“There was a history of him going to see his GP and seeking help with regard to the fact that he was lying,” says Mark Hensleigh. “It’s a very strange thing to go to your doctor and say, ‘I can’t stop myself lying.’”

Incredibly, a judge ruled that this was not enough grounds for appeal. It was only after Lynn recruited the help of a private detective to look further into the background of Danny Day, that they got the extra information they needed to beef up their case.

Day had said that the rape had changed the course of his life. He had been a top-drawer boxer before it happened. But this, also, was a lie.

In the documentary, the private detective reveals: “The potential was that Mr Day was such a skilled boxer that he could have got to the level of going to the Olympics to represent the country. That was a fairly big statement to make.

“As an amateur boxer, to get to any level of recognition, he’s going to have been a member of an ABA (Amateur Boxing Association) club. But nobody had heard of him.”

David’s defence was granted an appeal at the Royal Courts of Justice on 20 July 2016, in front of three judges, having been in prison for two and a half years.

Mark says: “It was probably over in 18 minutes – if that.

“Because they were reading out a judgement that had already been prepared.”



Almost four years after Danny Day posted the letter through David’s door, three judges concluded that the conviction was unsafe. It was quashed and he was released from jail.

Alex and Lynn drove to Dartmoor on the day of David’s release.

“We were waiting at the big wooden gates and literally he just appeared with a clear bag with all his belongings in, and he came out, the door was shut behind him, and that was it,” says Alex.

“We were laughing and crying but Dave, as usual, didn’t show much emotion. We drove down the road to a pub and had a lunch and a pint.

“When he came out of prison, people shook his hand, they gave him back the freedom of the town and he had a letter from the chief of the fire service saying he never doubted him,” adds Simon.

Sadly, having lost so much of his life, David then lost his wife. Lynn died eight months later from sepsis. A couple of years later, David was diagnosed with dementia.

“You could see a change in him after Lynn died,” says Alex. “She was his life. I mean, they did everything together. She was the force behind him, if you like.

“We were caring for him a lot at the beginning but he has 24-hour care now. He’s a lovely man, a gentle soul and he didn’t deserve what he got.



“The scary thing is that, if it could happen to David, it could happen to anyone.”

In 2020, Danny Day was charged with perverting the course of justice. He was convicted on one single count and given a nine-month suspended sentence.

David Bryant asked the Ministry of Justice for compensation for being wrongly imprisoned, but he is yet to receive any.

News.title: I covered Lin & Megan Russell’s hammer murders that shattered UK – 30 years on, I still have doubts on the killer
News.content:
THE RANDOM hammer murders of Lin and Megan Russell in the Kent countryside 30 years ago today were a grim national milestone.

A maniac bludgeoned mum Lin, 45, and daughter Megan, six, to death and left surviving daughter Josie, then nine, for dead on a bridle path just outside the village of Chillenden, on July 9, 1996.



Thirty years on the man who was convicted of their murder, Michael Stone, is attempting the clear his name by providing new DNA samples.

And having covered the case at the time, I still have doubts about whether he is guilty of the heinous murders.

Four years before the tragedy, 23-year-old Rachel Nickell, was fatally stabbed by a sexual predator in front of her two-year-old son Alex on Wimbledon Common, South West London.



After Rachel’s death, no woman felt safe in public, even when with their children and walking a dog.

However, the attack on Rachel occurred in London, albeit in a quiet and relatively peaceful part of the capital.

The ferocious hammer assault on Lin and her daughters happened in the heart of the garden of England, among picture-postcard Domesday villages in the most idyllic scenes imaginable.

It is an area of outstanding beauty where Lin and husband Shaun had chosen to live as a safe haven to bring up their daughters when he took a job as a lecturer at Kent University.

If such an atrocity could happen there, then it might take place anywhere in the UK.



Lin and the girls were attacked at around 4:20pm on 9 July 1996 as they walked home from Josie and Megan’s CofE primary school in the nearby village of Goodnestone, with pet dog Lucy in tow.

It was a 15-minute walk to their home, the achingly pretty Granary Cottage, in the neighbouring village of Nonington.

By bad luck, as it turned out, the family were later than usual that day after the girls attended a school swimming gala in Canterbury.

Shaun raised the alarm when he returned home that night from work and found his family absent.

The bodies of Lin and Megan were found just before midnight. Josie was discovered nearby clinging to life with severe head injuries. Family pet Lucy had also been battered to death.



Josie was taken to a specialist trauma unit at King’s College Hospital, South London, where police escorted Shaun to be with her.

An unfortunate mix-up meant that Shaun initially believed Josie had died with Lin, not Megan.

His initial relief at finding Josie alive was instantly shattered by the realisation that Megan was dead.



News of the horror broke the following lunchtime and I was dispatched to the scene, where the police had helpfully set up a media point at the Griffins Head in Chillenden.

Detective Chief Inspector Dave Stevens, the affable senior investigating officer, spoke to and updated journalists in the pub car park over the following days.

Though his uniformed colleagues rather tarnished police and media relations at one point by breathalysing people driving away from the scene.

In order to accommodate the large media presence, Stevens also held a briefing at Goodnestone primary school leading to the incongruous sight of burly members of the press perched on tiny chairs.



The crime scene itself – a clearing by a copse between cornfields – remained sealed off as forensic experts combed it for clues.

One journalist, the Daily Star’s Dick Durham, drew a parallel to those fields and a description of the ‘’rushing of the corn’’ at the end of Truman Capote’s masterpiece true crime novel In Cold Blood.

Capote intended it to signify that nature was greater than human tragedy but for me that stunning landscape was scarred by what had happened to Lin and her girls. A sinister aura hung over those sunlit corn fields during those days.

The investigation itself was struggling. Detectives describe the first 24 hours after a murder as the golden period.



But no obvious suspects were emerging. Shaun Russell was an obvious immediate suspect since multiple murders of family members are almost always domestic-related.

But even back then, Dr Russell was still seen on several CCTV cameras in Canterbury High Street at the time of the murders.

In an era in which police did not seek to rigidly control the press, Shaun Russell also spoke movingly to several of us at his home a week after the murders.

It was impossible not to be deeply moved by what Shaun was going through. The only thing that was keeping him going was his determination to be by Josie’s side.



Josie’s initial struggle for life and then her slow recovery became a national focus of hope.

Her trademark hats and brilliant smile captured in photos taken after she left hospital were symbols of the triumph of good over evil and testament to the skill of the surgeons who saved her.

Sun photographer Arthur Edwards and I were invited by Shaun to meet with Josie several months after she left hospital.

She cheekily gave Arthur quite a run-around, and Shaun later said it was the first time he had seen Josie laugh since the day their lives changed forever.



Over the next year I periodically visited Dave Stevens at the Kent murder team’s Nackington offices. He was always happy to have a natter and a cigarette outside.

But the breakthrough in the case did not come until after a Crimewatch appeal on the first anniversary of the hammer attack.

A psychiatrist came forward to say a client had spoken of smashing skulls like eggs.

The name of the client was Michael ‘Mick’ Stone, a heroin addict with an appalling history of violence and a low-level thief and robber.

At this point, the story moved from the pretty countryside of East Kent to the squalid shooting galleries of Gillingham and Chatham.



Stone was initially charged and held on suspicion of burglaries and, through an acquaintance, I was able visit him in prison on three occasions before he was charged with the murders.

I found him quite personable. He owned up to a catalogue of violent offences but was adamant he had nothing to do with the Chillenden murders, even saying whoever was responsible should be hanged.

In October 1998 he was found guilty of the murders of Lin and Megan, and the attempted murder of Josie, mainly on evidence of three apparent prison cell confessions.

I still remember his anguished cries protesting his innocence from the dock after the verdicts were returned and a haunting photo of him being driven away from the court continues to play on my mind.

It was an unsatisfactory conviction which was immediately undermined by the retraction of evidence by a prisoner about one of those three confessions.



A re-trial was held in 2001 at Nottingham crown court when a jury convicted him again based on cell confession testimony of one prisoner alone, Damien Daley.

Were the jury influenced by the heartbreaking detail of the evidence? Almost certainly. Did they convict the right man? I couldn’t honestly say so beyond reasonable doubt.

However, there was some evidence which potentially pointed to Stone’s guilt which was ruled inadmissible.

Josie was never able to pick out Stone at an identity parade. But after his re-trial conviction, she pointed to a bus pass picture of Stone in The Sun and told her father Shaun: “That’s him.”

On the day after the murders, he apparently went to the home of a friend named ‘Jill The Pill’ and burnt his clothes – though evidence from drug users must be taken with caution, especially around timings and dates.



One thing is certain: if Stone was guilty, he wasn’t in the area alone that day.

I was told that a burglary accomplice of Stone’s, a Scottish heroin addict, was seen crying hysterically outside a Chatham pub on the day after the murders.

Another junkie, a former girlfriend of Stone’s now clean and living a respectable life, told me that on the night before the jury convicted him Stone rang her from prison.

According to the woman, who was a truthful witness on many other areas of Stone’s life, he told her that “if I go down I’m taking the other two with me”. Interesting, but hardly compelling evidence.

New DNA tests with updated techniques are being carried out in the hope of establishing or confirming who the killer is and Stone is today supplying a new profile from prison. An odd thing in itself for a guilty man to do.



Thirty years on and there remain nagging doubts about the safety of Stone’s convictions which won’t go away.

News.title: Monaco bomber ‘lured to forest by spy & ex-cop before being killed in hail of bullets over fears she’d blow their cover’
News.content:
THE Monaco bomber was allegedly lured to a forest by a spy and ex-cop before being killed over fears she’d give up their identities.

Anastasiia Berezovska, 39, was accused of blowing up an oligarch and fleeing to Ukraine – before she was found dead just days after the attack.



Vadim Ermolaev, 58, his lover Anna Nasobina, 46, and their son Ariel, 13, were left severely injured in the explosion.

Berezovska was accused of working with accomplices.



But GUR military intelligence officer Vladislav Reut, 33, and Vitaly Zhikovich, 49, a security service (SBU) agent have now been arrested following the prime suspect’s shocking death.

Reut was allegedly conspiring with Zhikovich, a former police officer who is accused of owning a torture chamber.



Ukrainian prosecutors were today allowed to arrest the pair before they were charged with “intentional murder committed by a group of persons by prior conspiracy”.

The men are suspected of killing Berezovska after her return to Kyiv following the explosion in Monaco which wounded the tycoon.

Nasobina was severely injured in the blast, and both her legs were amputated in emergency surgery.

She is fighting for her life in hospital.



The young boy sustained minor injuries and is in stable condition, as is Ermolaev.

Reut reportedly told cops he and Zhikovich took Berezovska – who was wanted by Interpol – to a forest to “intimidate” her.

He alleged that the pair had only wanted to scare her as they were concerned she might panic and rat them out.

According to Reut, Zhikovich suddenly pulled out a pistol and shot her once in the back of the head.



When she fell, Zhikovich began repeatedly shooting her, the former SBU officer alleged.

When the former cop ran out of bullets, he allegedly changed the magazine and fired again five more times.

They allegedly buried the body in the woods and threw their weapons and phones into the water, according to local media.



Reut is seeking a plea bargain and has not admitted direct involvement in the murder.

He cooperated with investigators and helped law enforcement discover the body, it was claimed.

Earlier, he confessed to Berezovska’s murder, because of threats from Zhikovich, who he believed was an SBU officer.



It comes after extraordinary footage showed the Monaco bomber grinning and buying a power bank just hours before she allegedly planted the bomb.

CCTV clips shows Berezovska wandering into a shop in the French town of Beausoleil, just after 5pm on the day of the attack.

She walks in on her phone, then leans over the counter of the shop.

The suspect then buys the power bank that was seen in her hand in photos circulated by cops looking to track her down.

In Zhikovich’s basement, investigators are said to have found a dungeon resembling a torture chamber.



Ukrainian border guard chiefs say that when Berezovska returned to her home country on July 1, there were no flags from Interpol saying she should be detained.

The relevant notice was issued several days later.

She was allowed into the country and subsequently contacted Reut and Zhikovich and agreed to meet.

Ermolaev reportedly had a £112,000 bounty on his head, but it is not known who ordered the attempt on his life.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

There are suspicions that the bombing could be related to disputes over a call centre business in Dnipro which involved Ermolaev and his adult son Artur, 35.



Both Reut and Zhikovich have been remanded in custody and denied bail.

News.title: GK Barry reveals her hangover hacks, including dunking her head into a bowl of ice-cold water & an unusual playlist
News.content:
GK Barry has revealed the quirky hacks she uses to recover from a night on the town, including dunking her head into a bowl of ice-cold water and listening to an unusual playlist.

Discussing her post-night-out routine, after submerging her face, Barry tunes into music with frequencies designed to help her get through the day after a heavy evening.



Lifting the lid on her meticulous regime, Barry said: “What I do is I’ll wake up and start the day by lying to myself I’m fine.

“Then I’ll put on eye patches and dip my head in an ice-cold bowl of water. Two paracetamol, two ibuprofen, and I’m ready to attack the day. The world is my oyster.”



Discussing her other unusual recovery hacks, Barry teamed up with Tropicana Hydrate+ to deliver refreshments to Londoners, helping people get over those big late nights out for the football.

She added: “When I used to live in Nottingham, I’d have to get the train from Nottingham to London for work after a big night out.

“I’d have to listen to music on YouTube with frequencies that are supposed to help a sore head and hope it would help. And to be fair, on some of my darkest days, it did do something.”

Barry said she can sometimes overstep the mark when it comes to enjoying herself, adding: “I tend to think I’m more sober than I actually am – even when I am pretty loose.”



Recalling one particular night out, Barry revealed how a trip to Ibiza ended with her being hauled from a fountain by the Baggs brothers and Max Balegde.

She said: “I was in Ibiza and we went to this restaurant with lots of meats, cheeses and wine. Let’s just say I went a bit too heavy on the wine and too light on the meat.

“I ended up jumping into a fountain and nearly drowning. Thankfully I was rescued by my friends – including the Baggs brothers and Max Balegde.

“Then they had to carry me home – and to make things worse I dropped my phone in there.

“The next day I woke up looking like The Grudge. At least I was wearing a lovely pair of Hawaiian pyjamas, so every cloud has a silver lining.”



Barry also revealed she has been ‘loving’ this summer’s football, particularly the underdog stories of Cape Verde, Curacao and South Africa.

Helping struggling football fans recover from some late nights, Barry was seen refreshing members of the public with cooling face masks and Tropicana Hydrate+ pineapple and coconut water drinks.

And when it comes to surviving the late nights due to the awkward kick-off times, she urged fans to make sure they are getting enough kip around the games.

“I’d say make sure you sleep,” she said, “I’ve never understood it when people are like, ‘We’re going to have to ride it out.’ I have never been a ‘ride it out’ person.

“You need to go to bed, and you need to lie to yourself the next day you went to bed at 9pm. Make sure you chuck away your Oura Ring as well, which will tell you you’re going to suffer.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Barry is hopeful about England’s chances of progressing further through the tournament.

When asked if they could go all the way, she said: “God bless Harry Kane. A girl can dream!”

News.title: Scientists reveal real meanings behind creepy ‘witch marks’ found carved into historic English buildings
News.content:
SCIENTISTS have revealed the real meaning behind creepy so-called “witch marks” that are carved into historic English buildings.

Daisy wheels or hexafoils have been puzzling experts for years, but one historian says they have the answer.



Inside medieval churches and houses around the country, these intricate carvings have been puzzling historians for years.

Some believed them to be special symbols drawn on walls to offer protection.



But Professor Jennifer Alexander, a professor of architectural history at Warwick University, has set the record straight.

As the author of Stonemasons’ Marks, she says that the scribbles are simply marks left by stonemasons while they worked on the buildings.



She told The Guardian: “Do you remember at school when you were first given a pair of compasses and you made a daisy wheel? It’s that.”

“There are hundreds of such marks and they tend to be [of] varying degrees of skill.

“It’s much more the sort of thing you’d use to train apprentices with, giving them skills in using tools on intractable surfaces like stone.”

The marks are the stonemasons trying out different geometry and pattern designs with no evidence that they have any links to witches.



In 2016 Historic England could have possibly helped grow the belief that these marks were made by witches.

It urged the public to hunt for witches’ marks that “date back to times when belief in witchcraft and the supernatural was widespread”.

Its website states that the significance of hexafoils is disputed but still refers to them as witches’ marks, ritual protection symbols or apotropaic marks.

The website reads: “For example, the world of Wicca, which is a contemporary Pagan religious movement, sees them as sun motifs.

“Another school of thought suggests they are purely secular and could be geometric exercises for apprentices.



“However, their interpretation as a ritual protection mark is the most widely accepted theory at present.”

A 14th-century barn in Bradford-on-Avon in Wiltshire is one of the sites where these stonework symbols have been identified.

A previous survey by the public body that protect the historic environment, revealed that these symbols are common across England.

The research explained: “The most common mark recorded is the hexafoil, or daisy wheel, which range from the straightforward singletons to complex interlinked multiple examples.

“According to the public’s responses, they occur across the whole of England and on a variety of buildings from the medieval to the 19th century, including in houses, farm buildings and churches.



“It is of course impossible to be certain of the date of the marks but there are certainly much later examples, on 19th century buildings, than expected.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Historic England told The Guardian: “We welcome new research that adds to our understanding of these marks.

“The more we learn about them, the richer our picture of the people who made and used these places becomes.”

News.title: Bizarre final posts from ‘giga chad’ influencer Connor Murphy posing with tasers & swords just days before his death
News.content:
YOUTUBER and looksmaxxing influencer Connor Murphy – who drowned in Thailand after acting erratically – shared a series of strange social media posts before his death.

Connor, 32, trashed his apartment and ran away from police before jumping into a lake in Samut Prakan, 16 miles south of Bangkok.



Eyewitnesses claimed they heard him screaming and later saw him rolling on the ground outside his home with his hands clasped together, making religious remarks.

After the police were called on Tuesday, he fled and stripped naked before jumping into a 32-foot-deep lake by a golf course, according to the Bangkok Post.





Authorities struggled to reach him, and he eventually lost strength.

Divers from the Poh Teck Tung Foundation reportedly searched for about 30 minutes before they found his body roughly 20 meters from shore.

Full autopsy and toxicology findings are pending, and tributes have been pouring in for the self-styled “giga chad” – a meme term for a square-jawed alpha male.

Since the tragedy, odd social media videos have emerged showing him acting in a bizarre manner and playing with tasers and swords.



His last clip, posted to Instagram just four days before he drowned, shows him dressed up as an elf in a blue and green outfit with a red and black cape.

Connor is seen wearing fake elf ears and a messy blond wig as he runs around while two friends sit watching in the living room.

The Texas-born influencer was filmed wielding a toy bow and arrow in the alarming clip.

In another video shared on social media, Connor is seen wearing a neon green leotard with an unknown object on his head, while a male friend dressed in costume stands nearby holding a sword.

Connor appears to direct a scene, speaking with a woman before looking toward the camera and saying, “Action.”



Later in the clip, he seemingly accidentally activates a taser, recoiling in shock before staring at the camera and laughing.

He is also seen setting a small bush on fire while it sits on a table.

The group then bursts into laughter as Connor pretends to cast a spell with a magic wand, pointing it toward the camera.

The baffling video is captioned: “On the 1st day of Christmas my true love gay to me, a par fridge in a pair of trees,” including a golf emoji.

Other clips posted online show the influencer topless, wearing a large cape as he plays with swords and moves around in a dramatic fashion.



Connor’s rumored girlfriend, only known as Bee, had been staying with him at their once-lavish rental property and reportedly told police his behavior was out of character.

Images and video obtained by Asia Pacific Press show Connor’s home in a squalid condition after he vandalized it while his girlfriend slept in another room.

Bags of trash are seen in the images piled high in the kitchen and what appears to be black and yellow paint smeared all over the walls.



A black tar-like substance is also splattered across the sink area, while packets of the antidepressant Stablon are seen nearby.

The medication, which is used to treat major depressive disorder and anxiety, is not approved by the FDA for use in United States.

The psychotropic drug is available in Thailand but cannot be purchased over the counter and requires a medical evaluation.

Among the piles of trash found in his home were also packs of Falim gum, a Turkish sugar-free gum that has become popular among “looksmaxing” communities, as users believed constant chewing helps define the jawline.

Fellow looksmaxxer Androgenic wrote in an obituary on X, “He began meditating, taking psychedelics, and looking into spirituality and the concept of awakening, which I myself find fascinating.”



After his death, another video, believed to have been shared months ago, went viral, appearing to show him after he’d taken drugs.

“I feel like I’m dying every second,” he told his millions of followers on TikTok, as his eyes darted around the room.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I’m just making this video so I can watch it and remind myself, ‘Am I dreaming? Is it real?'”

Fellow YouTuber Call me Koosh described it as “last message to the world before his death,” as it was reshared on Tuesday.

News.content:
Iranian officials have accused the US of striking the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant after Donald Trump renewed attacks in the Middle East this week

News.title: Mummified sex offender found dead in a caravan after six months on the run
News.content:
The mummified body of a sex offender was found in a caravan six months after he became the subject of a police manhunt in connection with the death of his partner, an inquest has heard.

Richard Scatchard, 71, went missing after his partner, Kelly Faiers, 61, was found dead at his home in Minehead, Somerset, in October 2023.

An inquest into Ms Faiers' death held earlier this week heard that Scatchard coerced her into taking an overdose of sleeping pills and alcohol. The inquest concluded the mother of four, from Weston-super-Mare, had been unlawfully killed.

Scatchard was on life licence after being convicted of drugging and sexually assaulting women between 1986 and 2000. Somerset Coroner’s Court heard that the last confirmed sighting of Scatchard was in the Watchet area of Somerset - around 10 miles from Minehead - the day after Ms Faiers' body was found.

Image: Avon and Somerset Police/SWNS) Avon and Somerset Police/SWNS)

Avon and Somerset Police could not locate Scatchard and were unable to find evidence he was alive after October 2023. His body was found at a campsite in Watchet six months later when the caravan was removed from winter storage.

The inquest was told Scatchard, who was described as fit and well for his age and with no known medical conditions, was identified from fingerprints.

In a written statement, Detective Constable Mark Evison said Scatchard was wearing a wristwatch, which was set to British Summer Time.

"This was immediately thought of as being significant by inferring that the time on the device had not been altered since at least the October 29 2023," he said.

"While the police had been unable to locate Richard Scatchard, the UK has been following Greenwich Mean Time, but due to a recent change to British Summer Time on March 31, 2024, this would have corrected a clock back to the current time accuracy.

"Due to the mummified nature of his body, it’s highly likely that he died prior to March 31 2024, ultimately inferring that the watch was last set prior to October 29 2023, and so therefore would have passed prior to this date because he never corrected the watch to GMT."

Detective Sergeant Craig Thomson said Scatchard had no known links to the campsite and that it was not known how he had travelled there. "We do not know for certain what day he went into the caravan," he said.

He added that there was no evidence of any third-party involvement in his death or any intention to self-harm.

Pathologist Dr Deborah Cook carried out a post-mortem examination on Scatchard and said his body was "heavily decomposed". She said there were no visible signs of injury, no penetrating injuries and no evidence of self-harm.

"Post-mortem examination confirmed near-total mummification of the body," Dr Cook said. "The internal organs were severely affected by decomposition, but there was no obvious natural disease to account for his death."

She said there was evidence of fractures to five of his ribs, which would have been sustained close to the time of death.

"In an individual without pre-existing compromise to respiratory function, the probable effect of five rib fractures would be a degree of chest pain, a potential difficulty in taking deep breaths," she said.

"But five rib fractures would not be anticipated to cause death. With the degree of decomposition present, it’s not possible to exclude a concussive head injury having caused or contributed to death."

Image: Avon and Somerset Police/SWNS) Avon and Somerset Police/SWNS)

Toxicology samples showed the presence of alcohol and a compound found in sleeping tablets, cough medicine and hay fever medication.

However, due to the level of decomposition, it was not possible to obtain accurate samples for assessment, the court heard.

Dr Cook added: "Given the advanced state of decomposition with likely interval between death and post-mortem of over five months, it’s not possible to confirm or refute a hypothesis that death was due to sleeping tablet toxicity or to a combination of sleeping tablets and alcohol." She gave the cause of death as "unascertained".

The court heard Scatchard had kept his relationship with Ms Faiers secret from his probation officers as he was required to disclose "any emerging intimate relationships".

He had been given two warnings for breaching his licence conditions and had been told he risked being sent back to prison.

Probation officer Curtis Martin said Scatchard had been assessed as posing a medium risk. "He was assessed as being too argumentative and controlling with the professionals, and there were concerns that without these risk monitoring and controls being in place, he would be an increased risk towards the public," he said.

Samantha Marsh, senior coroner for Somerset, recorded an open conclusion on Scatchard’s death, saying there was no conclusive evidence to determine how or when he died.

"I accept he would have known undoubtedly he was going back to prison, and he would likely have been there for some time, which is a fact I think he would have also have been aware of," she said.

"In terms of findings, I find that there was no opportunity for the police to locate Richard alive earlier. He was someone who did not want to be found. I’ve got no evidence that he’s alive after October 16.

"On the evidence taken at its highest, I cannot determine how he came by his death. The date of death will be recorded in these circumstances as the date of discovery."

An inquest into Ms Faiers’ death held earlier this week concluded the mother-of-four, from Weston-super-Mare, had been unlawfully killed.

News.title: Nigel Farage live: Clacton voters blast Reform leader's 'weird' by-election plot amid Jenrick 'probe'

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage's vanity by-election appears to have spectacularly backfired with his only major challenger being a comedian who goes by the name Count Binface

Voters in Clacton slammed Nigel Farage's vanity by-election, branding him as "wasting money" that could set taxpayers back £200,000 all to see off a challenge from Count Binface.

BBC Breakfast viewers issue same complaints as Count Binface grilled live on air READ MORE :
