World.title: Writer, director and actor times two: Harvey Zielinski’s debut double act
World.content:
CultureMoviesAustralian film Writer, director and actor times two: Harvey Zielinski’s debut double act Karl Quinn July 9, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Harvey Zielinski’s first outing as a director is off to a flying start, with his film Sweet Milk Lake making its debut at Melbourne International Film Festival, which unveiled its 2026 program on Thursday night. Already the film is in the running for two of the richest prizes in the business – MIFF’s $140,000 Bright Horizons prize next month and the $100,000 Cinefest Oz prize in his home state of Western Australia in September. Harvey Zielinski, meet Harvey Zielinski: The actor-turned-director plays twins in Sweet Milk Lake. Justin McManus “It is amazing,” says the 35-year-old of this double dip in the potential prize pool. “It was quite mind-blowing to get that news back to back. That was a good week.” Sweet Milk Lake is a deeply personal work for Zielinski, who writes, directs, co-produces and plays two roles, as twin brothers Sam and Jake. It was a lot of hats to wear, and it made for an experience unlike any the actor-turned-director had ever had on a film set.



“It was exhausting. I didn’t sit down once for the entire shoot because there’s not a second in the day where you’re not needed,” he says. “That’s very different from being an actor.” The most difficult days were those in which the twins appear together – not actually, obviously, but through the old-school magic of split-screen photography. Zielinski played each character in turn, shot against a real backdrop to the halfway mark, and a body double appeared on the other half of the shot against a green screen. The whole thing would then flip, and the two performances were later edited together to create the impression that both brothers were present at the same time. Hunter Page-Lochard and Harvey Zielinski in Sweet Milk Lake. MIFF There are only a handful of such shots in the film, but they were, Zielinski says, “very challenging for my brain. I didn’t quite realise how fragmented I was going to feel on those days.” Fragmentation and doubling are at the heart of Sweet Milk Lake, which revolves around Jake’s decision to return to the country town where he grew up to visit his dying father Lee (Kieran Darcy-Smith). They haven’t seen each other for years – well, technically they haven’t seen each other ever because the last time they were together Jake was Sarah. Lee doesn’t even know his child has transitioned from female to male.



Related Article ★★★★

Melbourne live reviews Not crying Woolf: This production deserves to sell out, and probably will When Jake arrives, he is mistaken for Sam. In a split-second decision, he decides to let the confusion slide. He has many reasons, but key among them is the desire to experience a kind of masculinity that until this point he has only ever witnessed from the outside. Zielinski similarly transitioned himself at age 24, but says “none of the story is autobiographical”. The themes, though, are. “The kernel was that I was thinking a lot about [trans] visibility, about how you do all this work to transition and you think it’s going to be liberation – and in a lot of ways it is – but it’s not like people’s projections are going to stop coming. They’re just going to morph,” he says. “I was feeling frustrated about being pigeonholed [as a trans-masculine actor], the fact it was leading the conversation in every space I walked into – in fact, it was preceding me everywhere, professionally. People knew before I got there, and it was colouring everything. And I started thinking about what anonymity would look like if you moved to a town in the middle of nowhere and started again.”



Related Article ABC ABC’s new comedy tackles race issues like you’ve never seen before There’s freedom in that, but also alienation and risk, all of which his film explores, with subtlety and compassion. Zielinski began writing it during COVID, in a spirit of relative optimism about the level of acceptance and understanding around trans identity at the time. Were he to start the process today, he admits, he’s not sure he would come at it from quite the same place. “Perhaps naively, I just didn’t think it would get worse and not better. But it’s gotten so much worse,” he says. “This moment right now, politically, is an incredibly dark time for trans people around the world. We seem to be a group where it’s perfectly permissible to debate whether or not we should exist, which is quite unique. It has a really big impact on you on a day-to-day basis.”



His film is, he believes, hopeful, but it’s far from oblivious of the challenges trans people face in simply being accepted for who they are, not who others think they might or should be. “I’m not not optimistic,” he says. “But it would be remiss not to reflect on that.” Sweet Milk Lake screens in the Bright Horizons competition for first- and second-time filmmakers at MIFF. The festival runs from August 6 to 23. Full program: miff.com.au

World.title: Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed that made him ‘angry and rude’
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed that made him ‘angry and rude’ Rachel Rasker July 9, 2026 — 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

By the time Charlie Stowe’s father died at 63, he was already a “walking corpse”. “I never got to truly know who my father was,” the 19-year-old said. Stowe’s father, Richard, was diagnosed with early onset dementia at 53, when Charlie was just six years old. “Initially, he just lost his happiness and joy from everything, and then it was his speech, then his movement, his ability to eat solid foods, and then he started having strokes and seizures, until he passed away. “It was a relief to know that he was resting easy and we could remember him in the ways that we wanted to, before the disease.” Charlie Stowe will hike from Balgowlah to Newcastle in honour of his late father. James Brickwood



On Saturday, Charlie will embark on a 16-day hike from Balgowlah to Newcastle to honour his dad and to raise research funds and awareness for frontotemporal dementia, also known as FTD. In 2026, there were an estimated 29,000 people under 65 living with all forms of younger onset dementia, which is expected to increase to 41,000 people by 2054. Related Article Dementia Dementia is Australia’s leading cause of death. It’s even harder for people like Mithrani Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data released on Thursday revealed dementia is now the leading cause of death in Australia, overtaking coronary heart disease and accounting for almost one in 10 deaths. Over the past decade, the number of deaths caused by dementia has risen by 39 per cent. Of the estimated 450,000 Australians living with dementia, FTD affects less than 10 per cent and is most commonly diagnosed in 50-60 year olds.



FRONTIER Research Group clinician-researcher Dr David Foxe said the rarity of FTD can have “huge implications for diagnosis”, as can its symptoms – which do not typically involve memory loss. FTD is characterised by a build-up of abnormal proteins in the brain, causing brain shrinkage or atrophy over an extended period of time. Its most common subtype is a behavioural variant which causes people to become impulsive, socially inappropriate, apathetic or emotionally detached. Foxe said patients are often misdiagnosed with psychiatric disorders such as depression, and can “go around the garden path from doctor to doctor, not really knowing what the underlying problem is”. Stowe said the lack of awareness about FTD made his father’s condition socially isolating for his family. “You don’t hear about a 50-year-old healthy guy getting a disease like dementia,” he said. “A lot of our family friends cut him off because he was acting not like himself and [became] a rude and angry person.”



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Aaron lost three fingertips because of eczema. One injection could have spared him Stowe said studying for his HSC in 2024 became an “escape” from his personal life. Despite his father dying shortly before his trial exams, Stowe was dux of his grade, and plans to study law and environmental management at university – a passion he shared with his dad. “He was always adventurous – every Saturday we would do some hike,” Stowe said. “My aunty always said that despite his life being cut short, he had already lived five lives before then – he just made the most out of every single day.” The Sydney Morning Herald’s HSC Study Guide for 2026 will be published online and in the newspaper on July 27. The guide has all the information and tools to motivate and inspire the 80,000 students sitting the exam this year.

Related Article ABC ABC’s new comedy tackles race issues like you’ve never seen before There’s freedom in that, but also alienation and risk, all of which his film explores, with subtlety and compassion. Zielinski began writing it during COVID, in a spirit of relative optimism about the level of acceptance and understanding around trans identity at the time. Were he to start the process today, he admits, he’s not sure he would come at it from quite the same place. “Perhaps naively, I just didn’t think it would get worse and not better. But it’s gotten so much worse,” he says. “This moment right now, politically, is an incredibly dark time for trans people around the world. We seem to be a group where it’s perfectly permissible to debate whether or not we should exist, which is quite unique. It has a really big impact on you on a day-to-day basis.”



His film is, he believes, hopeful, but it’s far from oblivious of the challenges trans people face in simply being accepted for who they are, not who others think they might or should be. “I’m not not optimistic,” he says. “But it would be remiss not to reflect on that.” Sweet Milk Lake screens in the Bright Horizons competition for first- and second-time filmmakers at MIFF. The festival runs from August 6 to 23. Full program: miff.com.au

World.title: How a ceasefire may turn into a forever war
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters How a ceasefire may turn into a forever war July 9, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Trouble in the sky. Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. It’s deja vu all over again for US. It was the unwinnable Vietnam War in 1960s, Afghanistan’s 20-year war started in 2001 and now there is what looks like another “forever war” in Iran. Pete Seeger’s song Where have all the Flowers Gone? posed the question the Trump administration could well ponder, “When will they ever learn? When will they ever learn?“

Kevin Burke, Sandringham Trump is fighting the good fight with Iran

Despite his manifest faults, Donald Trump is justified in continuing to hold the Islamic Revolutionary Corps in Iran to account. As the NATO Secretary-General states, ″⁣When you have a ceasefire and Iran is basically violating the ceasefire, I think it is totally crucial that the US forcefully react″⁣. In removing more than 60 small boats of the Corps, the US is striking at Iran’s blackmail strategy in relation to the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s theocratic leadership must not now be allowed to rebuild its hold on a nation where its people, especially the youthful demographic, continue to be tortured physically and psychologically. Notwithstanding the claims of its delusional propagandists, Iran, without a viable navy and airforce and reeling from a broken economy, should now be perceived as a failing state. Washington should not relent, and the news that it has withdrawn a key concession that had allowed Iran to sell oil on international markets should be welcomed. This is a time when appeasement ploys should be discarded. For once, the US President can be on the right side of history. His military is fighting a ″⁣just war″⁣ in moral terms; and the people of the Middle East within and beyond Iran stand to benefit.

Jon McMillan, Mornington Waiting for our independence day

China tests a missile and we panic. The US tests one and we cheer them on. While China is making overtures about Taiwan and taking it over, look at what the US has done in the past couple of years – led a coup in Venezuela, unseating a president and plundering the oil reserves, blockaded Cuba and stopped it getting vital oil supplies, attacked Iran and disrupted the global economy. It cheered on Israel and its genocidal-like activities in the Gaza Strip and its invasion of southern Lebanon. Donald Trump indicated he wanted control of Greenland. He blocked much-needed arms supplies to assist Ukraine against Russia. The US put tariffs on us. We have got a dud deal with secondhand and new subs that we may never see. Who do we mistrust more? The US or China? If only we were an independent nation.

Greg Tuck, Warragul



The two sides to the American relationship

Like columnist Kate Allman (Comment, 9/7), I have spent considerable time in the US, and have many good memories and close friends. However the policies of the current Administration mean that I might be forbidden entry, primarily because of my writings about US politics and Israel. It would have been a stronger article had Allman reflected on the reasons many of us now, reluctantly, are not planning a visit.

Dennis Altman, Clifton Hill In these times, there are other places to go

I have visited the United States several times and fully agree with Kate Allman about its breathtaking beauty. And I appreciate the friendliness of many Americans, a few of whom have become my lifelong friends. However, individuals such as myself have limited ways of opposing attacks on human and civil rights, and serious threats to democracy in other countries. Boycotting is one of the available strategies. Visitors will gladly travel to the US when they can once more respect and trust its president and government. For the time being, many potential tourists, including myself, will stay well away and enjoy Australia and Europe, especially Spain.

Mirna Cicioni, Brunswick East In search of the makers of peace

Blessed are the peacemakers, but where are they?

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood THE FORUM Pothole factors

It isn’t just government maintenance shortfalls that cause plagues of potholes on country roads. (″⁣Potholes not just a bump in the road″⁣, 9/7). It is two entirely different suites of policies.

First, the tax structures that make it cheaper and easier to run SUVs as family cars, which result in much weightier cars in normal traffic conditions. Then, we begin paying the price for our governments’ lacklustre efforts in reducing greenhouse gas emissions – heatwaves, floods and storms, all affecting road surface integrity.

We now have a scenario where country people are coping with potholed roads by buying even bigger and heavier utes, which can only make a bad situation worse.

Colin Mockett, Geelong



Circle the danger

Having just returned from a trip to the Western Districts I can confirm the dreadful state of our highways and smaller roads. At the very least circle them with reflective paint so that we have a chance to avoid them in this ″⁣whack a mole″⁣ driving.

Denise Stevens, St Kilda Stay alert

The failure to keep both rural and suburban roads free of dangerous potholes has become a longstanding problem across Victoria. Poor road conditions have been normalised, despite the safety risks they create. While a speed limit sign may state 100 km/h, that is the maximum permitted speed, not the speed you must travel. If road conditions do not safely support that speed, slow down. Adjusting your speed to suit the conditions will help you and your vehicle reach your destination safely.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Idea has weight

Given the increase in the number of larger vehicles being used by people, and the increasing damage to roads in this state, would it not make sense to have the weight of a vehicle linked to the cost of the registration of such vehicles?

Jenny Camp, Moonee Ponds Rail is the answer

Columnist Chip Le Grand is correct in his appraisal of rural roads. As well as carrying out more maintenance on these roads, the government needs to pay more attention to removing heavy vehicles off roads by getting more freight on rail and to fast-track the gauge standardisation of broad gauge lines. Work has started on rebuilding the standard gauge Ararat to Portland line but much more across the state is required.

Rod Watson, East Brighton Beyond the pale

Senator Sarah Henderson, I realise that the Liberals are on life support, but dialling triple zero during the Telstra fail is beyond the pale — especially when others have more genuine needs.

Jenny Bone, Surrey Hills



Check the boom

Australia should stop pretending the data-centre boom is a harmless tech trend (“Green energy giants say data centre boom a win for nation”, 9/7). Last year, data centres alone drove half of the nation’s growth in electricity demand. Unless these hyperscale, AI-driven warehouses build more renewable generation and storage than they consume, they don’t power innovation but rather siphon off clean energy, strain the grid and increase climate pollution.

The Climate Council warns that data centres could push wholesale energy prices up by 23 per cent in Victoria by 2035. A moratorium on new developments until the Allan and Albanese governments impose real, enforceable standards is both sensible and necessary.

Letting data centres expand unchecked is not progress — it’s surrender.

Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn The passing signs

I see Pam the Bird from the train when I visit the CBD. Also I see the Free West Papua on the silos in Sunshine where I grew up. On my way to my first job as an office junior at The Age in 1973 I always enjoyed seeing the Flood Motors vehicle sign in West Footscray.

The Flood Motors sign is still there. Free West Papua is still relevant.

Billboards generally lack imagination and good design and are detrimental to enjoyable visual experience.

Gary Price, Castlemaine Creative work

Like it or loathe it, graffiti is more creative, more visually stimulating, funnier, cheaper, less intrusive and less ruinous to the planet than the obnoxious commercial advertising in our faces day and night throughout every urban centre in the country.

Paul Bucci, Geelong West It’s just scribble

A huge piece of scribble emblazoned on top of a pylon that can be seen from kilometres away is not street art.

The Bolte Bridge is public property, paid for by taxpayers, and is not a canvas for vandals.

By all means allow street art in the dirty laneways of inner Melbourne, where aficionados can marvel at wannabe Banksys to their heart’s content. The perpetrator of Pam the Bird is nothing more than a graffiti vandal and should be treated as such by the law.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully Test case

It’s interesting to note the fine distinction some individuals draw between “art” and “tagging”.

Perhaps the test should be: “would you allow your own home to be daubed with art or individual decoration without your consent?“

Peter Russo, West Brunswick



For the public good

Such an accurate observation from your correspondent in support of public art (Letters, 8/7). It’s good to hear from a new generation with the imagination to appreciate the potential value of the contribution that public artwork offers to the community.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor Simply vandalism

Surely the continuous repetition of the same image, eg: Pam the Bird or tagging, cannot be referred to as creative artwork. I’ll reckon there will be no Pam the Bird on a grandmother’s front fence, or tags on other so-called graffiti artists’ parents’ front fences. It is simply vandalism to alter the appearance of property that does not belong to you.

Peter O’Brien, Newport Social rankings

Your correspondent wrote (Letters, 8/7) ″⁣it was certainly dire for women in prior centuries as ... daughters had to marry to avoid homelessness. Otherwise they faced gruelling work in workhouses or being taken in by charities or family″⁣.

The fate of unmarried women in England in the 19th century would have been very different for each social class. For the wealthy and the middle class, ″⁣spinsters″⁣ would almost never have faced homelessness but would have found comfortable accommodation with a near or distant family.

Working class women would inevitably have been employed as servants or worked in factories or shops and would have lived in some form of lodging.

It would have been the poor who would have had no option but to turn to workhouses, rely on charities or be forced to turn to prostitution.

David Fry, Windsor Score this as a win

Your correspondent (Letters, 9/7) remarks on the fabulous excitement, compared to AFL, experienced by a soccer crowd when a goal is scored with everyone jumping up and down in unison given the rarity of these moments in a 90-minute game; and who can deny that in the context of a World Cup this is a fabulous thing?

But the main reason this looks so good is that team’s supporters are generally partitioned off from each other to ensure that they do not tear each other apart. In AFL, we sit with opposition supporters and with such frequent scoring no one has either the time or inclination to set off a flare.

Julian Guy, Mt Eliza Rein in abusers

Re the article ″⁣Europeans declare war on sick leave″⁣ (9/7), as a retired intensive care unit manager I used to tell my staff not to come to work while feeling unwell. Most of the time illnesses are viral and infective, which can easily be transmitted. Sick leave is expensive as it has to pay the the worker who takes the leave but also the replacement worker who often gets a higher rate of pay. There will always be some who abuse the system. It is these people who need to be reined in, not those who are genuinely ill.

Maria Liew, Woodend



Fragile systems

The frequent outages of crucial communication and management systems as well as data hacking events highlight the dangers of our ever-increasing reliance on these systems.

There does not seem to be much in the way of backup provisions, so that when a system goes down, we are left high and dry.

The adoption of these systems also leads to the loss of workers’ abilities to do the work of the systems manually, leaving us without alternatives.

The obvious fragility of modern computer technology and our dependence on it has to be regarded as a potentially dangerous weakness in our ability to function without it in emergencies.

An enemy would only have to knock out a few key elements and our society would grind to a halt.

Michael Meszaros, Alphington The Trump course

Donald Trump should run a TAFE course on Diplomacy 101 for aspiring diplomats.

Sandy Jeffs, Christmas Hills AND ANOTHER THING Graffiti

I love Pam the Bird. A beautiful and much-needed piece of whimsy. Leave her there and save the $70,000.

Wendy Batros, Templestowe It would have been more appropriate if the graffiti on the Bolte Bridge had been a pair of big ears.

Robin Jensen, Castlemaine



Nick Reece is definitely out of touch when he thinks Pam the Bird isn’t art and is an eyesore. Let the cool kids express their creativity even if it’s messy and not always polite. Beauty and art is in the eye of the beholder, it’s subjective.

Sally Walcock, Toorak Regarding Pam The Bird, the phrase “it might have been funny the first time” springs to mind.

Ross Bardin, Williamstown It is surely irrelevant whether billboards, big birds, and graffiti are art forms or not. What is publicly important is that they do not dominate the landscape, instead relegated to places where they can be enjoyed in private.

Peter Drum, Coburg Furthermore

Telstra outage puts V/Line trains out of action. Why doesn’t V/Line have some sort of back-up plan for this? It would help.

Doug Springall, Yarragon If they called the deplorable condition of Victorian country roads a ″⁣major event″⁣, it would get more attention from the state government.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill



Perhaps Australia should do its own missile test close to Chinese waters. I wonder what China’s response would be?

Garry Meller, Bentleigh Does anyone not see the irony of the prime minister lauding a deal to export uranium to India which will generate nuclear power and its banning on its use in Australia.

Martin Newington, Aspendale Is it time to give AI a new name? Automated Information surely gives a better description than the word artificial intelligence, which conjures up outer space vibes and deep suspicion.

Vivienne Whitehead, Paynesville

World.title: Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed that made him ‘angry and rude’
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed that made him ‘angry and rude’ Rachel Rasker July 9, 2026 — 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

By the time Charlie Stowe’s father died at 63, he was already a “walking corpse”. “I never got to truly know who my father was,” the 19-year-old said. Stowe’s father, Richard, was diagnosed with early onset dementia at 53, when Charlie was just six years old. “Initially, he just lost his happiness and joy from everything, and then it was his speech, then his movement, his ability to eat solid foods, and then he started having strokes and seizures, until he passed away. “It was a relief to know that he was resting easy and we could remember him in the ways that we wanted to, before the disease.” Charlie Stowe will hike from Balgowlah to Newcastle in honour of his late father. James Brickwood



On Saturday, Charlie will embark on a 16-day hike from Balgowlah to Newcastle to honour his dad and to raise research funds and awareness for frontotemporal dementia, also known as FTD. In 2026, there were an estimated 29,000 people under 65 living with all forms of younger onset dementia, which is expected to increase to 41,000 people by 2054. Related Article Dementia Dementia is Australia’s leading cause of death. It’s even harder for people like Mithrani Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data released on Thursday revealed dementia is now the leading cause of death in Australia, overtaking coronary heart disease and accounting for almost one in 10 deaths. Over the past decade, the number of deaths caused by dementia has risen by 39 per cent. Of the estimated 450,000 Australians living with dementia, FTD affects less than 10 per cent and is most commonly diagnosed in 50-60 year olds.



FRONTIER Research Group clinician-researcher Dr David Foxe said the rarity of FTD can have “huge implications for diagnosis”, as can its symptoms – which do not typically involve memory loss. FTD is characterised by a build-up of abnormal proteins in the brain, causing brain shrinkage or atrophy over an extended period of time. Its most common subtype is a behavioural variant which causes people to become impulsive, socially inappropriate, apathetic or emotionally detached. Foxe said patients are often misdiagnosed with psychiatric disorders such as depression, and can “go around the garden path from doctor to doctor, not really knowing what the underlying problem is”. Stowe said the lack of awareness about FTD made his father’s condition socially isolating for his family. “You don’t hear about a 50-year-old healthy guy getting a disease like dementia,” he said. “A lot of our family friends cut him off because he was acting not like himself and [became] a rude and angry person.”



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Aaron lost three fingertips because of eczema. One injection could have spared him Stowe said studying for his HSC in 2024 became an “escape” from his personal life. Despite his father dying shortly before his trial exams, Stowe was dux of his grade, and plans to study law and environmental management at university – a passion he shared with his dad. “He was always adventurous – every Saturday we would do some hike,” Stowe said. “My aunty always said that despite his life being cut short, he had already lived five lives before then – he just made the most out of every single day.” The Sydney Morning Herald’s HSC Study Guide for 2026 will be published online and in the newspaper on July 27. The guide has all the information and tools to motivate and inspire the 80,000 students sitting the exam this year.

World.title: Evacuate now: State of emergency declared for Wairoa due to flooding
World.content:
Wairoa Mayor Craig Little has declared a Local State of Emergency for the district.

The declaration at 11pm followed what Wairoa District Council called "significant flooding across the district, with rising river levels affecting homes, businesses, farms, roads and essential services."

Some communities have become isolated and "a number of residents have already been evacuated from affected areas to ensure their safety," the council said in a Facebook post.

"Declaring a State of Emergency allows emergency services and response agencies to work together quickly and effectively to protect people, coordinate resources, and support our communities as the situation continues to develop.

"If you live in a low-lying or flood-prone area and are concerned for your safety, please do not wait."

Second evacutation centre opens

At 12.10am, the council said on Facebook that Taihoa Marae, on the north side of the river, had been opened as an additional evacuation centre for residents.

The other evacuation centre is Wairoa War Memorial Hall.

"If you are in a low-lying or flood-prone area and are concerned for your safety, please do not wait. Leave early while it is safe to do so," the council's post said.

"If you know someone who may need assistance, please check in on them if it is safe to do so.

"Emergency services and response agencies will be heading out to assist with evacuations in flooded streets in Wairoa.

"Please continue to monitor conditions throughout the night. Please avoid unnecessary travel, follow all road closures, and never drive through floodwater."

Declaration follows alerts and warnings

Earlier on Thursday night, Wairoa residents received an emergency alert as floodwaters began to rise in low-lying areas.

People between Outram and Grant Streets, and Kopu Road and Apatu Street were advised to leave immediately, taking essential items and pets.

The council had said floodwater was beginning to come across Kopu Rd, and the road was closed in the Sturdee St area.

It comes amid an orange heavy rain warning for the ranges of Hawke's Bay, north of Napier, that is in place until 9am Friday.

MetService said: "Expect 100 to 130mm of rain on top of what has already fallen. Peak rates of 10 to 20 mmh expected today."

The council had previously warned residents to be ready to leave at a moment's notice - concerned about the lower catchment of the Wairoa River.

It said police will be door knocking properties in the area to ensure residents are aware of the changing conditions and to assist anyone who may need to evacuate.

Modelling showed overnight river risk

Following discussions with its flood modellers on Thursday evening, the council said there are increasing concerns that river levels could rise significantly overnight.

Its concern was the lower catchment of the Wairoa River.

"While the Wairoa River mouth is open, outgoing water and rising flow is competing against large 3m-4m swells coming in from the coast," it said.

"More water is also expected to flow into the Wairoa River from the upper catchments, with further heavy rain forecast overnight."

High tide was expected around 12.47am on Friday, with intense periods of rain until 3am.

Mayor Little said the emergency operations centre has been stood up and will be monitoring the situation through the night.
